registers.role: outcomes: childbirth / number of newborns, with parental person IDs

registers.role: worker demographics (population register information on persons)

variables_mentioned: product-level domestic production by eight-digit CN good
firm revenue share in quota products in 1999

linkages: Workers matched to firms through the employee–employer matched data of IDA; exposure is assigned from the 1999 firm's domestic production of quota goods
Marriage and divorce information from Denmark's Central Population Register matched to worker data with a unique person identifier
Childbirths linked to parents through the personal IDs of the Fertility Database
Partners (married spouse as well as cohabitant) linked to workers to control for partner earnings, income and import-competition exposure
Workers linked to the 1999–2009 change in Chinese import penetration through their six-digit industry of employment as of 1999

sample.universe: All persons of age 15–70 residing in Denmark with a social security number, all establishments with at least one employee in the last week of November of each year, and all jobs active in that week; from these, Denmark's 1999 private-sector labour force
sample.unit_of_observation: worker-year (quota experiment, 1994–2009); worker (economy-wide analysis of cumulative 2000–9 outcomes)
selection_rules: Workers who were between 18 and 56 years old in 1999 (so that workers would typically not retire during the sample period)
Employees who worked as a full-time employee in 1999 (so that female and male workers have comparably strong labour market attachment)
This yields a 1999 cohort of about 1.6 million workers (N = 1,651,774), essentially Denmark's entire private-sector labour force
Of these, about 10,000 were employed in the textile and clothing industry: the 'quota experiment sample' (4,743 exposed and 5,255 control workers)
Exposed = the 1999 firm had domestic production in an eight-digit CN good whose Chinese quota was lifted upon China's WTO entry; control = workers in other textile and clothing manufacturing firms
Subsamples used: fertile age (18–39 as of 1999), not fertile age (40+), single as of 1999, not married as of 1999, and workers with at least one family activity over 2002–9
sample.period: 1994–2009 (quota experiment panel); outcomes cumulated over 2000–9 in the economy-wide analysis
sample.n_observations: 153,137 worker-years in the main quota-experiment specification (Table 3, Panel B, Column 1); 138,497 in the Panel C specifications
sample.n_individuals: 1,651,774 private-sector workers; about 10,000 textile and clothing workers (4,743 exposed, 5,255 control); 24,797 single fertile-age textile workers; 64,768 textile workers not married in 1999

construction_notes: Earnings, income and hours are expressed in the worker's own average 1996–9 annual earnings, income and hours rather than in logarithms, so that zeros for non-employment can be kept
Employment is an indicator for being employed in a primary job in year t; a worker's annual labour market position is recorded at the end of November of each year

Unemployment is an index number of time in unemployment within a year (Table 3) and of total time in unemployment spells over 2000–9 in the economy-wide analysis, described in the text as measured in months
Personal income is labour earnings plus insurance payments and cash and non-cash transfers (including housing and utility subsidies); it differs from disposable income

Panel C outcomes are defined at the firm of employment in 1999 and take the value zero in years in which the worker does not work for that firm; pre-1999 years in which the worker was not at the 1999 firm are undefined and drop out
Exposure is an indicator defined on the 1999 firm; an alternative continuous exposure measure uses the firm's 1999 revenue share in quota products (Supplementary Appendix A.5.1)
IMP_j(i) = (M^CH_{j,2009} − M^CH_{j,1999}) / C_{j,1999}, with C_{j,1999} = production − exports + imports in six-digit industry j in 1999
Instruments use 1996 consumption levels (C_{j,1996}) and 1996 industry import shares, to address sorting in anticipation of import changes
Log earnings in Tables 1 and 2 are measured in 2000 Danish Kroner (the Table 1 mean is about 40,000 current US Dollar)
Fertile age is defined as 18–39 years old in 1999; family activity is defined as birth, marriage or parental leave
Cumulative outcomes in the economy-wide analysis are defined over 2000–9; Panel B versions are cumulated only while the worker remains in the initial six-digit industry

Occupations are the Danish version of ISCO (D-ISCO) at the four-digit level, about 400 job types; two-digit ISCO fixed effects are used as controls and four-digit interactions with year as a robustness check

claims.statement: Among all textile and clothing workers, exposure to the Chinese quota removal reduced annual earnings by 4.1% of pre-shock annual earnings per year on average over 2002–9, but the effect is not estimated precisely.

register_source.value: Domestic production database with product-level information for manufacturing establishments, linked to the employee–employer matched data of the Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA), Statistics Denmark; no register variable names given.

definition.value: Indicator interaction Post_t × Exposure_{i,99}: Exposure_{i,99} = 1 if the worker was employed in 1999 in a textile or clothing firm with domestic production of an eight-digit CN good whose Chinese MFA quota was lifted upon China's WTO entry (control workers are those in other textile and clothing firms); Post_t = 0 for 1995–2001 and 1 for 2002–2009.

timing.value: Exposure fixed as of the 1999 firm of employment; Post switches on in 2002, when China's MFA quotas were removed.

register_source.value: Employee–employer matched data of the Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA), Statistics Denmark; no register variable names given.

definition.value: Annual labour earnings from the worker's primary job, expressed in the worker's average 1996–9 annual earnings (not in logs).

timing.value: Annual, over the 1994–2009 worker panel; the coefficient is the average annual impact over 2002–9.

units.value: share of the worker's average 1996–9 annual earnings (average annual impact)

magnitude.interpretation: an average reduction in annual earnings amounting to 4.1% of pre-shock annual earnings across the years over the sample period

estimand.target_population: Textile and clothing workers of the 1999 cohort exposed to the removal of Chinese MFA quotas
estimand.time_horizon: average annual impact over the post-liberalization period 2002–9 (2002, the year the quotas were lifted, is year 0); the panel runs 1994–2009
estimand.formal_query: E[Earnings | do(ImpComp = 1)] − E[Earnings | do(ImpComp = 0)]

population.description: Workers of Denmark's 1999 cohort whose firm of employment in 1999 was in textile and clothing manufacturing — the 'quota experiment sample' of about 10,000 workers, 4,743 exposed and 5,255 control — followed over 1994–2009.
subgroups_defined: exposed vs control textile and clothing workers
fertile age (18–39 in 1999) vs not fertile age
workers with at least one family activity (birth, marriage or parental leave) over 2002–9
population.selection: Aged 18–56 in 1999 and employed as a full-time employee in 1999 in a textile or clothing manufacturing firm; exposure is defined by whether the 1999 firm domestically produced an eight-digit CN good whose Chinese quota was removed.

identification.source_of_variation: The removal of Multi-fibre Arrangement (MFA) quotas on China's textile and clothing exports to the European Union following China's entry into the WTO in December 2001: China benefited from Phases I–III in 2002 and from Phase IV in 2005, and a worker is exposed if his or her 1999 firm had domestic production of an eight-digit CN good whose Chinese quota was lifted. Neither Denmark nor China negotiated the creation or removal of the quotas.

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: in the absence of the quota removal, exposed and control textile workers would have followed the same trend in the outcome.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Pre-trend analysis: equations (1), (2) and (3) are estimated from 1994 onwards and the pre-2002 coefficients are close to zero and insignificant; 1999 balance of exposed and control workers (Table 1) and 1995 balance (Supplementary Appendix Table A2).

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation before the year in which treatment is defined: exposure is dated to 1999, several years before China's WTO entry, so that pre-2002 outcomes do not already respond to the anticipated quota removal.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Footnote 11 attributes the negative 2000 and 2001 coefficients to possible anticipation and gives this as the motivation for defining treatment in 1999.

implies_edges.from: Exposure_{i,1999} (quota exposure)

key_assumptions.assumption: Worker fixed effects absorb all confounding worker heterogeneity: the influence of any observed or unobserved worker characteristic as of 1999 that may be correlated with future exposure (occupation, education, unobserved ability, technological differences across firms) is eliminated, i.e. such heterogeneity is additive and time-invariant.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in the identification discussion; specifications augmented with differential annual time trends by four-digit ISCO occupation as of 1999 (Supplementary Appendix Table A14).

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference: control workers — employees of textile and clothing firms producing none of the quota-affected products — are themselves unaffected by the quota removal.

implies_edges.from: Exposure_{i,1999} (quota exposure)

threats_discussed: Earlier MFA quota removal phases for other developing countries in 1995 and 1998 could have generated differential trends between exposed and control workers
Increased trade integration with Eastern European countries in the second half of the 1990s
Anticipation effects: coefficients in 2000 and 2001 turn negative, which the authors attribute to anticipation of China's WTO entry

Concurrent shocks correlated with the trade shock, in particular technical change / computer and information communication technology and automation, which may hit female-dominated jobs differentially
Sample composition differences between men and women across occupations (e.g. women disproportionately clerks, men disproportionately managers)
robustness_checks: Pre-trend analysis: equations (1)–(3) estimated from 1994, with pre-2002 coefficients close to zero
Balance of 1999 characteristics of exposed and control workers (Table 1) and of 1995 characteristics (Supplementary Appendix Table A2)
Alternative exposure measure based on the firms' revenue share in quota products in 1999 (Supplementary Appendix A.5.1)
Differential annual time trends by four-digit ISCO occupation as of 1999 (Supplementary Appendix Table A14)
Results including part-time workers (available upon request)

estimation.specification: Equation (3): ImpComp = Post × Exposure, with worker and year fixed effects
estimation.clustering: Robust standard errors clustered at the level of the worker's firm of employment in 1999

definition.value: Change in import penetration from China over 1999–2009 in worker i's six-digit industry of employment as of 1999: IMP_j(i) = (M^CH_{j,2009} − M^CH_{j,1999}) / C_{j,1999}, where C_{j,1999} is 1999 consumption (production minus exports plus imports) in six-digit industry j.

timing.value: Industry of employment fixed as of 1999; the change in import penetration is measured over 1999–2009.

register_source.value: Employee–employer matched data of the Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA), Statistics Denmark; no register variable names given.

definition.value: Cumulative annual earnings of worker i over 2000–9 in any job, measured in units of worker i's 1999–1996 average earnings.

timing.value: Cumulated over 2000–9; treatment is the 1999–2009 change in import penetration.

units.value: units of the worker's 1996–9 average annual earnings, cumulated over 2000–9, per unit of IMP

estimand.target_population: Male workers of Denmark's 1999 private-sector cohort in industries whose Chinese import penetration rose
estimand.compliers: Not characterized by the paper: the estimate is identified from six-digit industries whose change in Chinese import penetration in Denmark moves with the China-driven import surge in eight other high-income countries and with low industry transport costs (OpenDist).
estimand.time_horizon: outcomes cumulated over 2000–9, i.e. 1 to 10 years after the 1999 baseline year, against the 1999–2009 change in import penetration
estimand.formal_query: d E[Earnings (cumulative 2000–9) | do(IMP_j)] / d IMP_j

population.description: Denmark's entire 1999 private-sector cohort: all full-time private-sector workers as of 1999 (N = 1,651,774, about 45% women), followed over 2000–9.
subgroups_defined: most exposed (top 5% change in import penetration) vs not exposed
population.selection: Aged 18–56 in 1999 and employed as a full-time employee in the private sector in 1999; exposure is the change in Chinese import penetration over 1999–2009 in the worker's six-digit industry of employment as of 1999.

identification.source_of_variation: Variation across six-digit industries in the 1999–2009 change in Chinese import penetration in Denmark (imports from China over domestic absorption), following the sudden expansion of Chinese production capabilities around its WTO accession, using variation within two-digit industries.
identification.instrument: HIP^CH_j = (OM^CH_{j,2009} − OM^CH_{j,1999}) / C_{j,1996}, the change in Chinese imports in eight high-income countries (Australia, Finland, Germany, Japan, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Switzerland and the US) over 1996 consumption (equation (6)); and OpenDist_j, the log of the weighted sum of bilateral distances to the import source countries with 1996 industry import shares as weights (equation (7)).

key_assumptions.assumption: Exclusion restriction: the instruments — the change in Chinese imports in eight other high-income countries and the industry's transport-cost measure OpenDist — affect Danish workers' outcomes only through the change in Chinese import penetration in Denmark, because China's exports are driven by China's own reforms and the global decline in trade costs.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as the identification condition; Hansen J over-identification tests reported in the tables, with p-values virtually always above 10%.

implies_edges.from: HIP^CH_j (change in Chinese imports in eight other high-income countries over 1996 consumption)
OpenDist_j (log weighted sum of bilateral distances to import source countries, 1996 shares)

key_assumptions.assumption: Instrument relevance: the instruments are strongly correlated with the change in Chinese import penetration in Denmark and have the expected signs.
key_assumptions.supported_by: First-stage coefficients in Supplementary Appendix Table A16; Sanderson–Windmeijer F-statistics reported in the table.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Extensive control set as of 1999, occupation fixed effects to address confounding technological factors, and two-digit industry fixed effects.

identification.source_of_variation: The removal of Multi-fibre Arrangement (MFA) quotas on China's textile and clothing exports to the European Union following China's entry into the WTO in December 2001: China benefited from Phases I–III in 2002 and from Phase IV in 2005, and a worker is exposed if his or her 1999 firm had domestic production of an eight-digit CN good whose Chinese quota was lifted.
